rows.title: How to Prepare Structural Steel for Intumescent Painting
rows.faq: [{"question": "What surface preparation standard is required for intumescent painting?", "answer": "The standard preparation requirement for intumescent painting on structural steel is Sa 2.5 (near-white metal) as defined in BS EN ISO 8501-1. Some manufacturers and fire engineers specify Sa 3 (white metal) for aggressive environments or high-risk applications, but Sa 2.5 is the baseline for the vast majority of commercial and industrial building projects in England and Wales."}, {"question": "Can intumescent paint be applied over existing paint?", "answer": "Only if the existing paint is confirmed compatible with the intumescent system by the coating manufacturer, is in sound condition with no delamination or corrosion, and was applied to a correctly prepared substrate. In most refurbishment scenarios, the safest approach is to blast back to bare metal and start the system from scratch. Applying intumescent paint over an unknown or incompatible existing coating will void the fire rating certification."}, {"question": "How long after shot blasting can intumescent paint be applied?", "answer": "Freshly blasted steel will begin to flash rust within 2\u20134 hours in humid conditions. The primer must be applied within this window. For large structural steel projects, the preparation and priming are typically carried out in sections to ensure the primer is applied before flash rusting occurs. Commercial Shot Blasting coordinates the blasting and priming sequence to eliminate this risk."}, {"question": "Does intumescent paint need a primer?", "answer": "Yes, without exception. The primer provides corrosion protection to the freshly blasted steel and acts as the adhesion layer for the intumescent coating. Applying intumescent paint directly to bare steel without a compatible primer will result in corrosion beneath the coating and will void the manufacturer's warranty and fire-rating certification."}, {"question": "What is the difference between thin-film and thick-film intumescent paint?", "answer": "Thin-film intumescent coatings (typically 300\u20133,000 microns DFT) are used for interior structural steel in standard commercial buildings and expand at a ratio of up to 50:1. Thick-film coatings (typically 3\u201320 mm DFT) are used for hydrocarbon fire protection in industrial, offshore, and petrochemical environments. For most commercial and industrial building structural steel in the UK, thin-film intumescent systems are specified."}, {"question": "Who can certify intumescent painting work in the UK?", "answer": "Intumescent painting contractors should hold third-party certification from a UKAS-accredited body. In the UK, the relevant schemes are FIRAS (Warringtonfire) and IFC Certification. Certified contractors are audited against BS 8000-15 and must maintain quality records for every project. Building control bodies and fire engineers increasingly require FIRAS or IFC certification as a condition of approval for higher-risk buildings."}]
